analysis.one_liner: Lets pharmacies and wholesalers import FDA-approved prescription drugs from Canada to lower U.S. prices.
analysis.headline: Introduced with bipartisan support in April 2002, the bill was referred to the Senate health committee and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ordered the government to write rules letting licensed pharmacists and wholesalers bring FDA-approved prescription drugs into the United States from Canada, where they sell for far less. It would bar drug makers from cutting off supply to pharmacies that import, and would let individuals bring in up to a 90-day personal supply from registered Canadian pharmacies. The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay U.S. retail prices for prescription drugs, especially people without insurance coverage. Importation would let them buy the same FDA-approved medicines at Canadian prices, which are typically far lower, and the bill's anti-discrimination provision was designed to stop manufacturers from simply refusing to sell to importers.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to issue regulations permitting pharmacists and wholesalers to import FDA-approved prescription drugs from Canada.
Prohibits manufacturers from discriminating against importers by giving foreign buyers better terms or restricting access to drugs permitted for importation.
Requires the Secretary to grant individuals a waiver allowing importation of up to a 90-day personal supply of FDA-approved drugs from registered Canadian sellers with a valid prescription.
Includes safety machinery: batch testing for authenticity, registration of foreign sellers, and authority to suspend importers on discovery of counterfeit or violative drugs.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, who would lose some ability to charge higher prices in the U.S. than abroad. Some of the savings would depend on Canadian suppliers continuing to sell into the U.S. market, which could put pressure on Canadian supply and prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill relies on another country's price-controlled market to hold down U.S. prices; if Canada restricts exports or raises its own prices, the savings shrink or disappear, and the bill does nothing about the underlying U.S.-only pricing gap.

The safety and compliance machinery is heavy: detailed documentation for every shipment, laboratory testing of batches, and foreign-seller registration, which regulators have historically argued is difficult to enforce against foreign supply chains.
Coverage is narrower than it sounds: controlled substances, biological products, infused drugs, and intravenously injected drugs are all excluded.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The price relief for consumers would have been real but modest and uncertain, since it depended on Canadian sellers keeping up supply and on manufacturers not finding workarounds. The bill took safety concerns seriously with testing and documentation requirements, but those same requirements could have limited how much importation actually occurred. It was a partial fix, not a broad solution to U.S. drug prices.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in April 2002, sent to the Senate health committee, and sat there without a hearing or vote until Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Sen. Byron Dorgan and eight original cosponsors, including two Republicans, introduced the Prescription Drug Price Parity for Americans Act on April 24, 2002.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day it was introduced.
Eleven senators cosponsored the bill: 8 Democrats, 2 Republicans, and 1 Independent.
The action history shows no further action after referral and two sets of sponsor introductory remarks; the bill died in committee when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose ability to charge higher prices in the U.S. than abroad remained untouched, and the committee leadership that kept the bill from reaching the Senate floor, where a bipartisan coalition had lined up behind it.

for.name: Sen. Byron Dorgan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: 2 of 49 Senate Republicans
for.role: Cosponsors (Sens. Olympia Snowe and Susan Collins)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making the coalition bipartisan from the start.

against.name: Sen. Judd Gregg
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill, letting it die in committee without any action.

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Brand-name drug makers and their lobby
against.what_they_did: Opposed reimportation legislation, arguing it endangered the drug supply and undercut the price structure that funds drug development.

sides.party_line_note: The 11 cosponsors included 8 Democrats, 2 Republicans, and 1 Independent, but the Republican-chaired health committee never acted on the bill and no roll-call was ever taken.

industries.note: The bill would let U.S. buyers pay Canadian prices for the same FDA-approved drugs and bars manufacturers from cutting off supply to importers. It directly targets the practice of charging Americans more than foreign buyers.
Licensed U.S. pharmacists and wholesalers would become the legal importers of lower-priced Canadian drugs, gaining a new supply channel and a cost edge over manufacturers' U.S. pricing.
Registered Canadian sellers would gain access to a large American customer base, though heavy U.S. demand could eventually strain Canada's own supply and prices.
